item.title: TechSpar: An Evolving AI Technical Interview Training System
item.description:
TechSpar: An Evolving AI Technical Interview Training System

TechSpar is a continuously evolving interview training system designed to make every practice session count by connecting specialized training, resume interviews, JD interview prep, real-time Copilot, and recording reviews into a continuous technical interview feedback loop. Unlike typical market tools that simply generate a static set of questions and end the session without tracking past performance or target company expectations, TechSpar shares a single long-term user profile, knowledge base, weakness tracking, and review scheduler across all of its features.

🧩 Core Features

  • 专项强化训练: Combines question banks, knowledge bases, historical weaknesses, and mastery levels to dynamically generate questions.
  • 简历模拟面试: Reads the resume and progresses through self-introductions, technical questions, project deep dives, and counter-questioning.
  • JD 定向备面: Deconstructs job descriptions, combining resumes and historical profiles to generate role-specific strategies and questions.
  • 实时 Copilot: Offers real-time ASR, follow-up direction prediction, response suggestions, risk warnings, and optional voiceprint role recognition.
  • 录音复盘: Transcribes short and long recordings, provides structured Q&A, and outputs per-question analysis and improvement suggestions.
  • 长期画像: Summarizes strengths, weaknesses, and training trajectories, scheduling reviews using the SM-2 algorithm.
  • 个人资料库: Imports PDF, DOCX, Markdown, and text to provide context for training and personal agents.
  • 数据迁移: Allows exporting and importing single accounts or administrator site-wide archives, with personal sensitive credentials excluded from default exports.

⚙️ Technical Requirements and Setup

  • Bun 1.3.14 or a compatible 1.3.x version
  • macOS, Linux, or Windows
  • Setup commands:
    • git clone https://github.com/AnnaSuSu/TechSpar.git
    • bun install --frozen-lockfile
    • cp .env.example .env
    • bun run dev:desktop
    • bun run pack:desktop
    • bun run dist:desktop
    • bun run dist:desktop:mac-arm64 (macOS Apple Silicon: DMG + ZIP)
    • bun run dist:desktop:win-x64 (Windows x64: NSIS installer)

🚀 Availability and Installation

  • Online trial address: https://techspar.cn
  • Pre-built macOS and Windows installers can be downloaded from GitHub Releases for use after logging in online.
  • The repository is configured for macOS DMG/ZIP, Windows NSIS, and Linux AppImage/DEB formats.
  • Self-built applications include Electron and the compiled Bun backend, meaning a separate Bun installation is not required at runtime.
  • Suitable for individuals preparing for technical interviews who want to continuously record their progress using tools.

#TechSpar #InterviewPrep #AIAgents #DeveloperTools

Source: AnnaSuSu/TechSpar

item.title: Canva Adds AI Off Button and Library Content Controls
item.description:
Canva Adds AI Off Button and Library Content Controls

Canva has introduced a new toggle that allows users to turn off its generative AI features. This update responds to user requests for control over the platform’s expanding array of AI-powered tools.

🔍 Overview

The new feature provides a way to disable Canva’s generative AI capabilities, including its chatbot for image generation and specific editing tools. Users can also adjust their content library preferences to prioritize human-created designs over AI-generated ones.

🧩 How it works

To turn off generative AI features, users navigate to Profile > Settings > Permission and toggle off Enable generative AI features.

Separately, users can choose to see less AI-generated content by going to Profile > Your account > AI personalization and turning on the option to show less AI content. When this option is enabled, human-created content appears first when searching through Canva’s library for templates, graphics, and other design elements.

⚙️ Key details

  • Disabled Features: The toggle turns off many AI features, including:
    • Magic Write
    • Magic Design
    • Magic Layers
    • Magic Edit
    • Dream Lab
    • Canva Code
    • AI Shapes
    • Magic Expand (AI photo-extending)
    • Image generation via Canva chatbot
  • Enabled Features: Some AI-powered tools remain active because they “make everyday tasks faster without generating anything new.” These include:
    • Background remover
    • Magic Grab tool (lets you select an object in an image and move it somewhere else)
  • Content Library: Canva states that a “small portion” of its library consists of AI-generated content. Any design using these elements will have an AI label in its metadata.

💡 Why it matters

Since Canva’s significant push into AI in 2023, some users have expressed frustration with the influx of AI features and requested ways to disable them. Canva has continued to expand its AI-powered image-editing suite, including a prompt-powered editing update in April and the launch of its first in-house AI model, Canva Craft, last month. This new control allows users to manage their experience with these tools.

#Canva #GenerativeAI #DesignTools #UserControl

Source: Canva adds an AI ‘off’ button

item.title: Databricks introduces bulk migration for converting BI reports to AI/BI Dashboards
item.description:
Databricks introduces bulk migration for converting BI reports to AI/BI Dashboards

Databricks has made a new feature generally available that allows organizations to migrate multiple Business Intelligence (BI) reports to AI/BI Dashboards in a single run. This capability addresses the limitations of the previous one-report-at-a-time flow, which was suitable for pilots but resulted in a months-long manual grind for organizations with hundreds of reports. The bulk migration agent can now process an entire folder of reports from a single command.

🔍 Overview

The migration agent reads source BI files, generates corresponding AI/BI Dashboards on Databricks, and maps them to a specified target catalog and schema. Instead of importing reports individually, users can process many reports together. This extends the existing Databricks AI/BI migration experience to support batch processing from a single command.

🧩 How it works

To use this feature, users must ensure that partner-powered AI features are enabled at both the account and workspace levels. The migration process involves preparing source files and triggering the bulk flow through specific commands or natural language prompts.

File Preparation:

  • Export Tableau or Power BI reports to supported file types: .twb, .twbx, .tds, .tdsx, .pbit, or .tmdl.
  • For Tableau workbooks connecting to published data sources, export the data source (.tds or .tdsx) and place it next to the workbook.
  • Place all BI report files into a directory within a Unity Catalog volume. Note that bulk runs only pick up files from volumes; dragging files directly into the chat is only for single-report imports.

Triggering the Migration:

  • Directory-based: Pointing the command at a directory triggers the bulk flow for all reports in that folder.
  • Natural Language: Users can request, “Migrate every Power BI report in /Volumes/finance/bi/reports to AI/BI Dashboards.”
  • Specific Files: Users can name specific files, e.g., “Migrate Tableau reports Dashboard1.twb, Dashboard2.twb in /Volumes/finance/bi/reports to AI/BI Dashboards.”

⚙️ Key details

The agent recognizes the batch, lists the found reports, and matches Tableau workbooks to their companion data source files automatically. It checks with the user if a pairing is unclear and prompts for the destination catalog and schema. Reports are queued and processed a few at a time, reusing existing Unity Catalog tables and views where possible before creating new ones.

Supported File Formats:

Format Source
.twb Tableau
.twbx Tableau
.tds Tableau Data Source
.tdsx Tableau Data Source
.pbit Power BI
.tmdl Power BI

Execution and Monitoring:

  • Each report runs through the Genie Code planning phase, including parsing, assessing the workbook, enumerating the semantic layer, creating metric views, building dashboard pages, and validating the migration.
  • A status card in the chat maintains a running tally of the batch, marking each report as Queued, Running, or Completed.
  • Users can stop an individual report or halt all in-flight processes from the status card.
  • Each report runs in its own background job, so the tab does not need to remain open. Progress can be viewed later in Genie Code history.
  • If a run stops to ask a question, users can answer it in the linked Genie Code conversation, and the migration will pick up where it left off.
  • Every Genie Code response can be undone as a single step.

🚀 Availability

The bulk migration feature is now generally available and ready to use in workspaces today. For current limits on the number and size of files supported in a single bulk import, users should refer to the public documentation on /importBI.

💡 Why it matters

This feature transforms the migration of legacy BI assets into a strategic modernization effort that is no longer limited to manual, report-by-report grinding. By allowing organizations to point the agent at an entire folder, they can convert large libraries of reports to AI/BI Dashboards efficiently, ensuring that metric views and SQL views are mapped to the correct target catalogs and schemas.

#Databricks #AI-BI #DataMigration #GenieCode #BusinessIntelligence

Source: Bulk migrate your dashboards to AI/BI with Genie Code

item.title: CueSplat: Efficient Dynamic Scene Rendering on Edge Devices
item.description:
CueSplat: Efficient Dynamic Scene Rendering on Edge Devices

CueSplat, a post-training framework, enhances dynamic scene rendering by leveraging local temporal regularity in Gaussian trajectories. It predicts Gaussian attributes from recent history and uses a lightweight router to select deformation updates within a scene-specific budget, achieving significant speedups on edge devices with minimal quality loss.

🔍 Overview

  • CueSplat is a post-training framework that exploits local temporal regularity in Gaussian trajectories for dynamic scene rendering.
  • It predicts Gaussian attributes from recent history and uses a lightweight learned router to select deformation updates within a scene-specific budget.
  • The framework keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and retains its Gaussian set.

🧩 How it works

  • CueSplat predicts Gaussian attributes from recent history and uses a lightweight learned router to select exact deformation updates within a scene-specific budget calibrated offline.
  • Selection accounts for prediction reliability and rendering contribution.
  • Selected indices are reused across nearby frames to reduce routing overhead.
  • To control accumulated prediction error, CueSplat uses drift signals to schedule three consecutive full-deformation frames that rebuild the prediction history.

⚙️ Key details

  • CueSplat achieves up to 6.74× and 8.15× speedups on Jetson AGX Orin and Orin NX, respectively.
  • The quality drop is negligible, with at most 0.16 dB in dataset-average PSNR.
  • Evaluated across four mainstream 4DGS algorithms.

💡 Why it matters

  • CueSplat addresses the compute-intensive nature of deformation networks for all Gaussians at every frame on edge devices.
  • It retains the pretrained backbone and Gaussian set, making it a post-training framework.
  • The lightweight router and reuse of selected indices across frames reduce routing overhead.
  • The use of drift signals to schedule full-deformation frames helps control accumulated prediction error.

#DynamicSceneRendering #EdgeDevices #4DGS #CueSplat #AI

Source: CueSplat: Learning to Schedule Sparse Deformation for Dynamic Gaussian Splatting on Edge Devices

item.title: Decision models turn LLMs into structured classifiers
item.description:
Decision models turn LLMs into structured classifiers

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, a decision model that treats a large language model as a structured classifier rather than a free‑form generator.

🔍 Overview

  • Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text.
  • We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more.
  • Decision models shift from token‑by‑token generation to assigning probabilities to answers the application already understands.

🧩 How it works

  • Fundamental interface: State + Questions + Allowed Answers → Decisions + Probabilities.
  • A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities.
  • Example pipeline call: decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide").
  • Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.
  • Constrained decoding (e.g., using Outlines or XGrammar) can enforce JSON schemas, but it adds computational overhead.

⚙️ Key details

  • TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model; the community now uses the term decision model to describe this computational role.
  • The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).
  • Many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.
  • Conventional classifiers have a fixed head: adding a new label (e.g., a fourth department such as Legal) requires modifying the head, collecting data, and retraining.
  • Zero‑shot classification addresses this limitation by supplying candidate labels at inference time. Example: classifier = pipeline("zero-shot-classification", model="facebook/bart-large-mnli").
Pipeline Model
decision autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide
zero-shot-classification facebook/bart-large-mnli

💡 Why it matters

  • When an application only needs to choose between predefined answers, autoregressive decoding can be unnecessary work.
  • Because the model selects from allowed answers, it reduces the risk of producing invalid JSON, unexpected keys, or answers outside the allowed choices.
  • This approach is useful for routing customer‑support requests—determining which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

#DecisionModels #LLM #ZeroShotClassification

Source: Decision Models in Hugging Face

item.title: DharmaOCR Field Extractor: 2B‑Parameter Model Beats LLMs on Structured Document Extraction
item.description:
DharmaOCR Field Extractor: 2B‑Parameter Model Beats LLMs on Structured Document Extraction

A new 2‑billion‑parameter model called the Field Extractor, built on the DharmaOCR‑LITE v1.1 checkpoint, extracts exactly the fields you ask for from any document image and returns typed JSON. It outperforms every frontier large language model (LLM) we tested while costing a fraction of the price.

🔍 Overview

  • Takes a document image (invoice, ID, contract, court filing, etc.)
  • Returns structured JSON: each field typed (string, number, boolean) and nested where the document nests
  • Works on any language supported by the training data (English, Portuguese, and other European/Asian languages)

🧩 How it works

  • OCR layer – First runs OCR to obtain the full printed text, preserving original layout.
  • Two request modes
    • Open – No schema supplied. The model infers label‑value pairs and tables from layout and context, returning every detected field as key‑value pairs.
    • Schema‑directed – You provide an exact schema (field names and types). The model fills the schema, returns null for missing fields, and produces no extra keys, so the output can be piped directly into downstream systems.
  • Output is always valid JSON with typed values.

⚙️ Key details

  • Base model: DharmaOCR‑LITE v1.1, a 2‑billion‑parameter model optimized for OCR via supervised fine‑tuning and DPO.
  • Adapter: LoRA adapter trained on 43,384 examples covering both request modes.
  • Training data:
    • English multi‑domain documents collected from the public web.
    • Brazilian documents in Portuguese sourced internally.
    • Smaller multilingual set covering other European and Asian languages.
    • All data annotated at the field level.
  • Benchmark: 546 documents across three scenarios (open extraction, partial schema, schema with nonexistent fields) – 1,638 total cases.
  • Metric: Field‑level F1 (matched by path, including table position) multiplied by Levenshtein similarity and JSON validity.

📊 Performance comparison

Provider Quality gap (F1 pts) Cost factor vs Field Extractor
Claude Opus 5 (closest) 1.8 ~6× higher
GPT‑5.6 Luna (widest) 9.3 ~147× higher

The Field Extractor achieves higher accuracy while running at dramatically lower cost because it processes only the necessary tokens for OCR and field extraction, unlike general‑purpose LLM APIs that require full‑sentence reasoning for every request.

🚀 Availability

You can try the Field Extractor yourself [here].

#OCR #DocumentAI #LLMComparison

Source: Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

item.title: NVIDIA releases France and Belgium locale‑grounded persona datasets for post‑training LLMs
item.description:
NVIDIA releases France and Belgium locale‑grounded persona datasets for post‑training LLMs

NVIDIA and French AI startup Pleias released Nemotron-Personas‑France and Nemotron-Personas‑Belgium, locale‑grounded persona datasets that enable post‑training of open language models for country‑specific accuracy.

🔍 Overview

  • AI adoption is expanding globally, and people across languages and cultures are using it in more aspects of daily life.
  • General‑purpose language models provide a powerful foundation but can lack local knowledge, cultural nuance, and precision needed for specific applications.
  • Post‑training can adapt an open model to these needs, improving accuracy and usefulness while supporting safer interactions.

🧩 How it works

  • Each persona is a synthetic resident grounded in regional demographic, geographic, linguistic, and cultural distributions.
  • A grounded persona includes an age, commune, job, and household that follow French census data, plus written profiles of the person’s work and daily life.
  • For Belgium, the persona dataset spans Dutch, French, German, and English.
  • The datasets are used to generate synthetic conversations for post‑training, covering more of the people the agent will serve.
  • Facts in each answer are taken from official procedure text and paired with each persona during the workflow.

⚙️ Key details

  • Locale‑grounded persona datasets for 12 countries are part of the open NVIDIA Nemotron data program.
  • Nemotron-Personas‑France and Nemotron-Personas‑Belgium were built with Pleias; the Belgian dataset also involved KU Leuven.
  • The Nemotron repository provides steps for data generation, training, and evaluation based on the NVIDIA NeMo open training stack.
  • Pleias uses three Nemotron‑Personas datasets, including France and Belgium, in its work on Lamina, a spine‑care assistant.
  • Pleias says, “Better grounded data is what makes a small efficient regional‑specific model viable.”
Persona Dataset Country Languages Covered Demographic Basis
Nemotron-Personas‑France France French French census data (age, commune, job, household)
Nemotron-Personas‑Belgium Belgium Dutch, French, German, English Belgian demographic data

🚀 Availability

  • The datasets are released as part of the open NVIDIA Nemotron data program, allowing developers to adapt open models market by market.
  • Developers can swap in another released persona dataset (e.g., Belgium) and keep the same behavior contract and review workflow.

💡 Why it matters

  • Example: A French passport‑agency agent answered a health‑related travel‑restriction question with an unspecific, unsupported response that conflicted with official documentation.
  • Using Nemotron‑Personas‑France, the correct answer references the official procedure: a home visit by a government official, a medical certificate, and online or municipal submission options.
  • Accurate, locally‑grounded responses improve user trust and ensure compliance with regional regulations.

#NVIDIA #LanguageModels #Localization

Source: Fine-Tuning NVIDIA Nemotron to Know Local Rules, Not Just Local Languages | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: New Multi‑Level Encoder with Global Topic Model Boosts Task‑Oriented Dialogue Summarization
item.description:
New Multi‑Level Encoder with Global Topic Model Boosts Task‑Oriented Dialogue Summarization

A new model called MLEGT (Multi‑Level Encoder with Global Topic) has been introduced to improve task‑oriented dialogue summarization.

🔍 Overview

  • Task‑oriented dialogue summarization automatically extracts key information to generate domain summaries.
  • The goal is to improve service efficiency and quality.

🧩 How it Works

  • Multi‑level encoder discovers temporal and spatial dependencies in dialogues.
  • During graph construction, the encoder simultaneously obtains a simple yet effective global topic.
  • A global topic‑guided pointer mechanism is added to the summarizer to capture ignored but important information, enhancing summary accuracy.

📊 Evaluation

  • A comprehensive study was conducted on two public datasets:
    • A real‑world large‑scale Chinese police interrogation dataset.
    • A medical reporting service dataset.
  • Results prove the superiority of the MLEGT method over several strong baselines.

#TaskOrientedAI #DialogueSummarization #MLEGT

Source: Multi-level Encoder with Global Topic for Task-oriented Dialogue Summarization

item.title: MarketBeat updates news sentiment scoring and coverage metrics
item.description:
MarketBeat updates news sentiment scoring and coverage metrics

MarketBeat has refreshed its real‑time news sentiment platform, providing clearer scoring for headlines and new comparative coverage data for individual companies.

🔍 Overview

  • Extended trading is trading that happens on electronic markets outside of regular trading hours.
  • This is a fair market value extended hours price provided by Massive.

⚙️ How it works

  • Each headline receives a score ranging from 2 (good news) to -2 (bad news).
  • Company news sentiment scores track the average news sentiment of articles about each company over the most recent 7 days to identify firms receiving positive press.
  • The system tracks news headlines from hundreds of news outlets and tags them by company.

📊 Key Metrics

Company Sentiment Score Sector Avg Sentiment Articles This Week Avg Articles per Week
MKTX ▼ 0.48 ▲ 0.58 (Average Finance News Sentiment) ▼ 5 ▲ 6
CCS ▼ 0.58 ▲ 0.42 (Average Consumer Discretionary News Sentiment) ▼ 8 ▲ 3
  • MKTX sentiment is below the finance sector average, with fewer articles this week than its typical weekly count.
  • CCS sentiment is also below its consumer‑discretionary sector average, and article volume this week is lower than the usual weekly volume.

📈 Media Coverage Comparison

  • A chart compares the number of articles about each company in the last seven days with the average number of articles for a typical week.
  • The platform highlights when coverage deviates up or down, helping investors spot changes in media attention.

📱 Stay Informed

  • Sign up for MarketBeat’s free daily newsletter to receive the latest news and ratings for these companies and their competitors.
  • SMS alerts are available in multiple countries (Australia, Belgium, Canada, etc.) and include stock alerts, news stories, and partner offers. Message and data rates may apply; you can unsubscribe at any time.

#MarketBeat #SentimentAnalysis #FinanceNews
